title: Taking Reinforcement Learning Cross Datacenter — Nan Jiang, Modal

primary.label: Post-Training & Continual Learning
primary.rationale: The video's central problem is distributing the RL post-training loop across datacenters. The core technical insight (Adam absorption) concerns how Adam optimizer steps during RL post-training interact with serving precision (BF16/FP8). The architectural solution (lossless weight patches, bulletin board, sidecar) is designed specifically to enable cross-datacenter RL post-training. The talk frames everything around the RL post-training loop, analyzes optimizer step dynamics during post-training, and proposes infrastructure for continual RL post-training across distributed GPU capacity. This matches the inclusion criterion: primary focus is fine-tuning, preference optimization, or continual learning systems.

secondary.label: Inference & Model Systems
secondary.rationale: The talk extensively analyzes serving precision formats (BF16, FP8, NVFP4, MXFP4) and their quantization rounding boundaries, discusses rollout serving engine compatibility (SGLang, vLLM, HF safetensors), and presents a serving-side architecture (bulletin board, sidecar proxy, version-aware engines). The precision/quantization analysis and rollout engine integration are core technical pillars of the talk.

secondary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
secondary.rationale: Modal's Stitch is presented as a concrete developer platform—framework-agnostic about trainer, engine, and transport; async-first and agentic-first. The talk describes infrastructure that other ML engineering teams build upon for distributed RL post-training, fitting the substrate-other-engineers-use criterion.

secondary.label: Orchestration & Durable Execution
secondary.rationale: The bulletin board architecture (immutable version publication, pull-based sync, no RDMA required) and sidecar coordination (proxy if current, apply transitions if behind, return not-ready if cannot catch up) are durable execution and coordination patterns for managing versioned state across distributed, failure-prone systems.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: Stitch is a developer platform/tool used by ML engineers and builders for distributed RL post-training. The talk is addressed to platform engineers and ML infrastructure teams who build on this substrate.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The Adam absorption technique and lossless patch mechanism are applicable to any RL post-training scenario regardless of downstream application domain. The talk is not specific to any vertical and the technique generalizes across model providers and research labs.

summary: Nan Jiang (Modal) presents a solution to the cross-datacenter RL post-training bottleneck: frontier-scale checkpoints (~500 GB) take minutes to hours to ship over commodity links, making sub-second weight updates impossible. He argues the full checkpoint is the wrong synchronization unit and proposes that fewer than 1% of rollout-visible (served BF16/FP8) weights change between consecutive policy versions. The key insight is Adam absorption: at RL post-training learning rates (~3e-6), the per-parameter Adam push is over 1000x smaller than the BF16 rounding boundary (~0.0039), so FP32 master weights move but served BF16 values remain bit-identical. This is not gradient sparsity—gradients are ~99% nonzero and dense; the updates are simply too small to cross the precision floor. The shipped object is a lossless bitwise patch (~500 MB), not a floating-point delta, enabling exact bitwise-identical reconstruction with no additive drift. Lower-precision serving (FP8, NVFP4, MXFP4) sharpens absorption further. The architecture uses a bulletin board: the trainer publishes immutable weight versions after each optimizer step; rollout engines living outside the training cluster pull and materialize versions locally in HF safetensors format, compatible with SGLang, vLLM, etc. A sidecar makes any engine version-aware—proxying if current, applying missing transitions if behind, returning not-ready if it cannot catch up. This enables elastic rollout where any idle GPU across regions and providers joins the fleet. Modal's implementation, Stitch, is framework-agnostic, async-first, and agentic-first. Open questions remain: whether absorption holds for Muon optimizer, how scalable fully async RL is, and whether the paradigm generalizes to pre-training, mid-training, and SFT.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts in this talk are inseparable: the entire system architecture (bulletin board, sidecar, lossless patch encoding, elastic fleet) exists to exploit a single AI insight—Adam absorption. The BF16 rounding boundary and Adam step dynamics create the technical opportunity (fewer than 1% of served weights change), and the engineering patterns (immutable version publication, pull-based sync, bitwise reconstruction, graceful degradation) are the means to operationalize it. Without the precision-floor analysis, the engineering architecture has no motivation; without the bulletin board and sidecar, the absorption insight has no practical deployment path. The talk is a case study in how a deep understanding of floating-point representation and optimizer dynamics directly drives distributed system design, and conversely how system architecture choices (serving precision, version negotiation, checkpoint layout) are shaped by ML training dynamics. This interdependency is what makes the talk significant: it bridges numerical analysis, optimizer theory, and distributed systems engineering into a single coherent production system.
temporalContext: This talk was published on August 10, 2026, on the AI Engineer YouTube channel. Research was conducted as of August 23, 2026. At the time of the talk, Modal had recently raised a $355M Series C (May 2026) at a $4.65B valuation and had published the RL infrastructure blog post in June 2026. The Training Gym SDK and the StitchRecipe PR (modal-projects/training-gym/pull/219) were publicly available. The talk references GLM 4.7 Air (a Zhipu AI model) and discusses the Muon optimizer as adopted by Moonshot and DeepSeek—both active research directions as of mid-2026. The cross-datacenter RL post-training paradigm described represents the frontier of distributed ML infrastructure research at the time of publication.
takeaways: The full checkpoint (~500 GB at frontier scale) is the wrong unit of synchronization for cross-datacenter RL; it takes minutes to hours to ship and kills low-latency weight updates.

Fewer than 1% of rollout-visible weights change between consecutive versions (~99% bit-identical per step)—not because gradients are sparse (they are ~99% nonzero and dense), but because Adam steps are too small to cross the BF16 rounding boundary.

Adam absorption: BF16 rounding boundary is ~0.0039 for weights near 1; typical Adam step at RL post-training LR is ~3e-6, over 1000x smaller, so served weights do not change even though FP32 master weights move.
The shipped object is a lossless bitwise patch (~500 MB), not a floating-point delta, enabling bitwise-identical reconstruction with no additive drift.
Lower-precision serving sharpens absorption further: FP8 serving of GLM 4.7 Air saw 0.15% weight change on first step, settling near 0.05%; group-scaled formats like NVFP4 follow similar rationale.
The bulletin board architecture decouples trainer and rollout: trainer publishes immutable weight versions; rollout engines pull and materialize locally, requiring no RDMA connection to the trainer.
A sidecar makes any rollout engine version-aware—proxying if current, applying missing transitions if behind, returning not ready if it cannot catch up—enabling elastic global rollout.
Stitch is Modal's concrete implementation: framework-agnostic, async-first, agentic-first; scattered inference capacity becomes one elastic rollout fleet.

Open questions remain: whether absorption holds for Muon optimizer, how scalable fully async RL is, and whether the paradigm generalizes beyond RL post-training to pre-training, mid-training, and SFT.

concepts.name: Adam absorption
concepts.explanation: At RL post-training learning rates (~3e-6), the per-parameter Adam update is over 1000x smaller than the BF16 rounding boundary (~0.0039), so FP32 master weights move but served BF16 values remain bit-identical. This is the core technical insight that enables sparse weight patches.
concepts.importance: This is the foundational AI insight that makes the entire cross-datacenter RL architecture possible—without it, full checkpoints would remain the only synchronization unit.

concepts.name: BF16 rounding boundary (ULP)
concepts.explanation: The precision floor for served weights: BF16 spacing is approximately theta/128, with the nearest rounding boundary at ~theta/256 (~0.0039 for a weight near 1). If the master FP32 weight moves by less than this boundary, the served BF16 value does not change.
concepts.importance: Defines the threshold that Adam steps must exceed for a served weight to change. Understanding this boundary is essential for predicting absorption behavior across model architectures and weight magnitudes.

concepts.name: Cross-datacenter RL post-training
concepts.explanation: Distributing the RL post-training loop across datacenters by decoupling rollout serving from the trainer cluster, enabling use of scattered GPU capacity that cannot be co-located in a single tightly coupled cluster.
concepts.importance: This is the problem the entire talk addresses, and its solution has implications for how ML teams architect distributed training infrastructure.

concepts.name: Served-weight sparsity vs gradient sparsity
concepts.explanation: Gradients are dense (~99% nonzero) and FP32 master updates are also dense, but served-weight sparsity (~99% bit-identical per step) arises from precision absorption, not from sparse gradients. This is a crucial distinction that prevents misattribution of the sparsity phenomenon.
concepts.importance: Prevents a common misconception: the sparse patches are not due to sparse gradients or sparse optimizer updates, but due to the interaction between dense small updates and low-precision serving. This distinction affects whether the technique generalizes to other optimizers.

concepts.name: Lossless weight patch
concepts.explanation: A bitwise diff of the served dtype-cast view comparing consecutive weight versions, encoding changed indices and their new imprint values. It enables exact reconstruction of the served version without floating-point additive drift.
concepts.importance: The practical mechanism that turns the absorption insight into a deployable synchronization primitive, reducing payload from ~500 GB to ~500 MB.

concepts.name: Rollout serving island
concepts.explanation: The movable architectural unit in RL post-training: a coherent endpoint serving one policy version that can scatter across commodity capacity because there is no cross-island all-reduce. The interface is simply policy version in, trajectory and metadata out.
concepts.importance: Identifies which part of the RL loop can be decoupled from the trainer cluster, which is the key architectural decision enabling cross-datacenter deployment.

concepts.name: FP8 serving and absorption
concepts.explanation: Lower-precision serving sharpens absorption: an internal Modal run serving GLM 4.7 Air in FP8 saw 0.15% weight change on the first step (higher LR), settling near 0.05% as Adam stabilizes.
concepts.importance: Empirically validates the absorption theory and shows that the trend favors the industry move toward lower-precision serving, making the technique more effective over time.

concepts.name: Group-scaled quantization formats (NVFP4, MXFP4)
concepts.explanation: Lower-precision formats with hierarchical scales that sharpen absorption: for fixed-point formats, visibility is roughly theta/2^(mantissa+1), so lower precision means fewer weights change per step. Group-scaled formats like NVFP4 follow similar rationale.
concepts.importance: Shows that the absorption phenomenon strengthens as the industry moves to even lower precision formats, extending the technique's relevance to next-generation serving stacks.

concepts.name: Muon optimizer (open research question)
concepts.explanation: An optimizer adopted by Moonshot and DeepSeek for which it remains an open question whether the Adam absorption analysis holds, since the talk only covers Adam. The speaker explicitly flags this as an open question.
concepts.importance: Identifies the boundary of the technique's applicability and a concrete research direction, which is important for learners evaluating whether to apply the approach with non-Adam optimizers.

concepts.name: Adam optimizer step dynamics at post-training LRs
concepts.explanation: Adam's per-parameter push is bounded by roughly the learning rate. At RL post-training LRs (~3e-6), this push is small enough to be absorbed by the BF16 precision floor, creating the sparsity that enables lossless patches.
concepts.importance: Connects optimizer theory to the practical synchronization mechanism, showing why the technique is specific to post-training LRs and may not hold at pre-training LRs.

concepts.name: Bitwise reconstruction of served weights
concepts.explanation: The rollout engine reconstructs a bitwise-identical served version from the lossless patch. Because the patch is bit-level equivalent (change index plus imprint value), not a floating-point addition, there is no additive drift over successive versions.
concepts.importance: Guarantees correctness of the served policy across many successive patches, which is essential for RL training stability over long runs.

concepts.name: Checkpoint as wrong unit of synchronization
concepts.explanation: A frontier-scale checkpoint (~500 GB) takes minutes to hours to ship over commodity links, making sub-second weight updates impossible. The full checkpoint includes optimizer states and FP32 master weights that are not needed by rollout engines, making it the wrong granularity for cross-datacenter sync.
concepts.importance: The framing that motivates the entire technical contribution—identifying the right synchronization unit (sparse served-weight patches) instead of the wrong one (full checkpoints).

concepts.name: Bulletin board architecture
concepts.explanation: A decoupled publish-subscribe pattern where the trainer publishes immutable weight versions to a shared store after each optimizer step, and rollout engines pull versions locally without requiring RDMA or direct connections to the trainer cluster.
concepts.importance: This is the core architectural pattern that enables cross-datacenter RL by decoupling trainer and rollout scheduling, eliminating the need for fast interconnect between them.

concepts.name: Sidecar pattern for version-aware serving
concepts.explanation: A sidecar proxy intercepts requests to a rollout engine, checks the engine's current weight version, and either proxies requests (if current), applies missing weight transitions (if behind but can catch up), or returns not-ready (if it cannot reach the target version).
concepts.importance: Makes any existing inference engine (SGLang, vLLM) version-aware without modifying the engine itself, enabling elastic fleet composition and graceful degradation.

concepts.name: Lossless bitwise patch encoding
concepts.explanation: Encoding technique that ships a change-index-plus-imprint-value diff of the served dtype-cast view comparing consecutive weight versions. Selective overrides and XOR are mentioned as encoding options. It is bit-level equivalent, not a floating-point addition, so there is no additive delta drift.
concepts.importance: Reduces synchronization payload from ~500 GB to ~500 MB while guaranteeing bitwise-identical reconstruction of the served version, making seconds-scale cross-region sync possible.

concepts.name: Immutable version publication
concepts.explanation: The trainer publishes weight versions as immutable artifacts after each optimizer step, ensuring that rollout engines can safely pull any version without coordination or locking.
concepts.importance: Eliminates distributed coordination complexity; any engine can independently and safely consume any published version at any time.

concepts.name: Graceful degradation in distributed serving
concepts.explanation: When a rollout engine cannot catch up to the target weight version, the sidecar returns 'not ready' rather than serving stale weights, providing a clean, explicit failure mode instead of silent inconsistency.
concepts.importance: Ensures correctness under heterogeneous fleet conditions where some engines may be slower or on lower-bandwidth links, without serving incorrect policy versions.

concepts.name: Elastic fleet composition
concepts.explanation: The architecture enables any idle GPU across regions and providers to dynamically join the rollout fleet, treating scattered inference capacity as a single elastic resource pool.
concepts.importance: Directly addresses the core problem that GPU capacity is distributed across providers, regions, price points, and availability, turning the 'bazaar' of scattered compute into a unified rollout fleet.

concepts.name: Framework-agnostic integration design
concepts.explanation: Stitch is designed to work with any trainer framework, serving engine (SGLang, vLLM), attention backend, parallelism strategy, GPU, and transport, maximizing portability across the ML ecosystem.
concepts.importance: Avoids lock-in to any single training or serving framework, making the system adoptable by diverse ML engineering teams with existing infrastructure.

concepts.name: Pull-based synchronization over push
concepts.explanation: Rather than pushing weights over RDMA from trainer to rollout engines, rollout engines pull weight versions from the bulletin board on their own schedule, decoupling trainer and rollout timing.
concepts.importance: Eliminates the need for a fast interconnect between trainer and rollout, which is the fundamental constraint that prevents cross-datacenter RL in the standard loop.

concepts.name: Checkpoint layout materialization
concepts.explanation: Rollout engines materialize pulled weight versions locally in checkpoint layout (HF safetensors format), ensuring compatibility with existing serving infrastructure like SGLang and vLLM without custom weight loading code.
concepts.importance: Bridges the patch-based synchronization to standard serving workflows, avoiding the need for engines to understand patches directly.

concepts.name: Bidirectional version negotiation
concepts.explanation: Requests carry version information bidirectionally: the requester specifies which version it wants, and the response includes which version was actually accepted, enabling correct trajectory attribution back to the trainer.
concepts.importance: Ensures that the trainer can correctly attribute rollout trajectories to the policy version that generated them, which is essential for correct RL gradient computation.

sections.title: Where the GPUs actually are & the standard RL loop
sections.summary: Introduces the mismatch: usable GPU capacity is distributed across providers and regions (the bazaar), but the default RL post-training loop forces everything into one tightly coupled cluster (the cathedral). RL simultaneously wants enough GPU, same region, fast fabric, and availability now. The standard loop couples rollout to the trainer cluster via fast RDMA weight sync, inheriting the hardest capacity constraints.

sections.title: The rollout serving island as the movable unit
sections.summary: Argues that backpropagation and collectives must stay in the trainer cluster, but the rollout fleet can leave. The movable unit is the rollout serving island—a coherent endpoint or local group serving one policy version. Across islands there is no global all-reduce; the interface is simply policy version in, trajectory and metadata out. The remaining dependency is weight synchronization.

sections.title: Why a full checkpoint is the wrong unit of sync
sections.summary: A frontier-scale checkpoint (~500 GB) takes minutes to hours to ship over commodity links, making sub-second weight updates impossible. For async or fully async training, weight update latency must be within seconds. The full checkpoint is therefore the wrong unit of synchronization.

sections.title: The bet: under 1% of served weights change
sections.summary: Proposes that fewer than 1% of rollout-visible weights (served BF16 or FP8, not FP32 optimizer states) change between consecutive versions. If true, only the diff of the served view needs shipping—shrinking the link from hundreds of GB to hundreds of MB—with bitwise-identical reconstruction of the served version.

sections.title: Ingredient one: the precision floor
sections.summary: Explains the BF16 precision floor: the optimizer keeps high-precision master weights, but the served view is BF16 with spacing ~theta/128. The nearest rounding boundary is ~theta/256 (~0.0039 for weight ~1). If the master weight moves by less than this boundary, the served BF16 value does not change.

sections.title: Ingredient two: the size of an Adam step & Adam absorption visualized
sections.summary: Adam's per-parameter push is bounded by roughly the learning rate. At RL post-training LRs (~3e-6), the push is over 1000x smaller than the BF16 boundary (~0.0039). Master weights move but served BF16 values do not—this is Adam absorption. Small weights on the left of the magnitude axis can still move; larger weights on the right are absorbed.

sections.title: Shipping a lossless patch, not a delta
sections.summary: The shipped object is a lossless bitwise diff of the served (dtype-cast) view comparing version t-1 and t. Encoding options include selective overrides and XOR. It is bit-level equivalent, not a floating-point addition, so there is no additive delta drift. The rollout engine reconstructs the exact served version. Full-parameter deltas are small by absorption; LoRA deltas are small by construction.

sections.title: Measurements, not gradient sparsity & lower-precision formats
sections.summary: Measurements show ~99% bit-identical per step; the patch is lossless (change index plus imprint value reconstructs the exact version). Gradients are dense (~99% nonzero) and FP32 master update is dense—it is just small. Lower-precision serving (FP8, MXFP4, NVFP4) sharpens absorption: for fixed-point formats, visibility is roughly theta/2^(mantissa+1), so lower precision means fewer weights change. Group-scaled formats like NVFP4 use hierarchical scales but follow similar rationale.

sections.title: Internal run on GLM 4.7 Air in FP8
sections.summary: An internal run serving GLM 4.7 Air in FP8 shows 0.15% weight change on the first step (higher LR), settling near 0.05% as Adam stabilizes. The pattern generalizes across different research labs and model providers using Adam in post-training.

sections.title: The bulletin board architecture
sections.summary: The trainer publishes immutable rollout weight versions to a shared bulletin board after each optimizer step. Rollout engines live outside the training cluster—no RDMA required—potentially in different regions or providers. Requests carry version information bidirectionally (which version requested, which version accepted), and responses return tokens, log probs, replay information, and metadata as if co-located. The trainer writes versions after optimizer state updates; engines pull, materialize locally in checkpoint layout (HF safetensors), and serve directly. Compatible with SGLang, vLLM, and any compatible attention backend, parallelism strategy, and GPU.

sections.title: The sidecar that makes engines version aware
sections.summary: The sidecar makes a normal rollout engine version-aware: if already at an acceptable commit version, it proxies requests; if behind but can catch up, it applies missing transitions; if it cannot reach the target, it returns not ready. This supports elastic rollout—any idle GPU can join the aggregated rollout fleet.

sections.title: 500 GB down to 500 MB & Stitch
sections.summary: Using the lossless patch instead of a full checkpoint reduces transfer size from ~500 GB to ~500 MB, enabling cross-region sync in seconds. Stitch is Modal's concrete implementation: framework-agnostic about trainer, engine, and transport; async-first and agentic-first. On the trainer side it publishes weight version definitions; on the rollout side it pulls latest weights and syncs across regions and providers. Scattered inference capacity becomes one elastic rollout fleet.

sections.title: Open questions: Muon, fully async RL, and beyond
sections.summary: Three open questions: (1) Does absorption hold for Muon optimizer (adopted by Moonshot, DeepSeek) since the analysis so far only covers Adam? (2) How scalable is fully async RL now that global compute is accessible? (3) Does the paradigm generalize to pre-training, mid-training, and SFT? Modal is hiring.

limitations: Adam absorption argument applies to full-parameter RL post-training with Adam at typical learning rates; extremely high learning rates or unusual optimizer configurations could change the sparsity ratio
Whether absorption holds for Muon optimizer remains an open question
Scalability of fully async RL is an open-ended question
Whether the paradigm generalizes to pre-training, mid-training, and SFT is unexplored

organization.name: Modal
organization.summary: Modal (Modal Labs, Inc.) is a serverless cloud computing platform built for AI workloads, founded in 2021 by Erik Bernhardsson and Akshat Bubna. The company built its own container runtime, file system, and scheduler from scratch in Rust, enabling sub-second cold starts and autoscaling from zero to thousands of GPUs. Modal pools GPU capacity across multiple cloud providers (AWS, GCP, Oracle, neoclouds) and is headquartered in New York City with offices in Stockholm and San Francisco. The company has raised over $483M in total funding, including a $355M Series C at a $4.65B valuation in 2026, and employs approximately 128 people. Customers include Suno, Cognition, Physical Intelligence, and Chai Discovery.

technologies.label: Adam absorption
technologies.summary: Adam absorption is the core numerical insight that at RL post-training learning rates (~3e-6), the per-parameter Adam update is over 1000x smaller than the BF16 rounding boundary (~0.0039), so FP32 master weights move but served BF16/FP8 values remain bit-identical for ~99% of parameters per step. This is not gradient sparsity—gradients are dense (~99% nonzero) and the FP32 master update is also dense—but the updates are too small to cross the precision floor. Lower-precision serving (FP8, NVFP4, MXFP4) sharpens absorption further. An internal Modal run serving GLM 4.7 Air in FP8 showed 0.15% weight change on the first step, settling near 0.05% as Adam stabilizes. Whether absorption holds for the Muon optimizer (adopted by Moonshot, DeepSeek) remains an open question.
technologies.role: Core technical insight—the entire talk builds upon this phenomenon to justify sparse weight patches, the bulletin board architecture, and Stitch as Modal's solution.

technologies.label: Lossless bitwise weight patching
technologies.summary: The lossless bitwise weight patch is a diff of the served dtype-cast view comparing consecutive weight versions, encoding changed indices and their new imprint values. Encoding options include selective overrides and XOR. It is bit-level equivalent, not a floating-point addition, so there is no additive drift over successive versions—the rollout engine reconstructs the exact served version. Full-parameter deltas are small by absorption; LoRA deltas are small by construction. This reduces the synchronization payload from ~500 GB (full checkpoint) to ~500 MB (sparse patch), enabling seconds-scale cross-region weight sync.
technologies.role: The practical encoding mechanism that turns the absorption insight into a deployable synchronization unit, reducing payload size by ~1000x and enabling seconds-scale cross-region sync.

technologies.label: Bulletin board architecture with version-aware sidecar
technologies.summary: The bulletin board architecture decouples the trainer and rollout fleet: the trainer publishes immutable weight versions to a shared store after each optimizer step, and rollout engines living outside the training cluster pull and materialize versions locally in HF safetensors format—no RDMA required. A sidecar makes any existing engine version-aware: proxying requests if current, applying missing weight transitions if behind but can catch up, or returning not-ready if it cannot reach the target version. Requests carry version information bidirectionally for correct trajectory attribution. This eliminates the need for fast interconnect between trainer and rollout, enabling elastic global rollout where any idle GPU across regions and providers joins the fleet.
technologies.role: The system architecture that enables cross-datacenter RL by decoupling trainer and rollout scheduling, eliminating RDMA dependency, and enabling elastic fleet composition from scattered GPU capacity.

technologies.label: Stitch
technologies.summary: Stitch is Modal's concrete implementation of cross-datacenter RL rollout weight synchronization. It is framework-agnostic about trainer, engine, and transport; async-first and agentic-first. On the trainer side it publishes weight version definitions after each optimizer step; on the rollout side it pulls latest weights and syncs across regions and providers. The system combines three core mechanisms: Adam absorption-based sparse weight patches (~500 MB vs ~500 GB), a bulletin board architecture for decoupled pull-based synchronization, and a sidecar for version-aware serving. It integrates with the Training Gym SDK, supports the slime RL framework, and is compatible with SGLang and vLLM serving engines via HF safetensors checkpoint format. Scattered inference capacity becomes one elastic rollout fleet.
technologies.role: Modal's flagship implementation presented as the solution to cross-datacenter RL; the talk culminates in its description as the system that turns scattered inference capacity into one elastic rollout fleet.

evidence.excerpt: the full checkpoint is a wrong unit of synchronization
evidence.supports: Full checkpoint is the wrong unit of sync for cross-datacenter RL

evidence.excerpt: What if less than 1% of rollout visible weights got changed from one version to another one
evidence.supports: Fewer than 1% of rollout-visible weights change between consecutive versions

evidence.excerpt: the near surrounding boundary is about 00039
evidence.supports: BF16 rounding boundary is ~0.0039 for weight near 1

evidence.excerpt: a typical added step here is around 3 millions so the update is more than a thousand smaller than the boundary
evidence.supports: Adam step (~3e-6) is over 1000x smaller than BF16 boundary

evidence.excerpt: there are multiple lossless encoding. People can do selective overrides. They can people can also do xor. The important part is like there are bit equivalent bit level equivalent
evidence.supports: Lossless bitwise patch encoding with no additive drift

evidence.excerpt: The paper reports the gradients are dense. About 99% of the parameter gets non-zero gradients. The FP32 master update is also dense. It's just small.
evidence.supports: Gradients are dense (~99% nonzero); served-weight sparsity arises from Adam absorption, not gradient sparsity

evidence.excerpt: we serve like GM 4.7 air in FP8 and we can see in the beginning there are only like 0.15% of weights got changed in the first step
evidence.supports: FP8 serving of GLM 4.7 Air: 0.15% weight change on first step, settling near 0.05%

evidence.excerpt: the trainer saying a cluster after it got updated it publishes immutable rollout based version to a shared bulletboard rollout engine leave outside of the training cluster
evidence.supports: Bulletin board architecture: trainer publishes immutable versions; rollout engines live outside training cluster

evidence.excerpt: the psychar just apply the missing transition. If they cannot get there the the psychar just simply return not ready
evidence.supports: Sidecar makes engines version-aware: proxy, apply transitions, or return not ready

evidence.excerpt: we can decrease the number of like transfer transfer size from like 500 gigabytes to 5 500 megabytes
evidence.supports: Transfer size reduced from ~500 GB to ~500 MB, enabling seconds-scale sync

evidence.supports: Open question whether absorption holds for Muon optimizer
